x86g9r:219: In the past year or two, AI has been rolling out within companies fairly quickly, but frontline employees generally report that AI output is often only half-finished. It's not that the model is inadequate; it's that it can't see the tone of that meeting, can't see the proposal that was rejected in that argument. Two years ago, a wave of AI hardware appeared on the market—worn around the neck, clipped to a collar, placed on a desk—attempting to solve the problem of individual data collection. But almost none of these products succeeded. The fundamental reason is that the entry point was wrong: all kinds of AI hardware were trying to solve data collection at the individual level, relying on the individual user's awareness—remember to wear it, remember to turn it on, remember to organize, remember to sync. Organizational-level data collected with individual-level devices is destined to be fragmented.
xijt0o:362: This has a long tradition in management theory. Netflix's Reed Hastings has the principle of "Context, not Control": good managers should not control every step of how employees work, but should fully provide employees with strategic goals, market context, and decision-making background. Drucker said that the essence of a knowledge worker's job is judgment, and the quality of judgment depends on how much information they have. Stanley McChrystal's "shared consciousness" in Team of Teams is also about letting frontline combat units see the same full picture that top command sees. This school of management has essentially been solving the same problem all along: how to put the right information in the right people's hands. AI in the enterprise is actually a continuation of this problem—it is a non-human knowledge worker, and what determines the quality of its output is not just how well the prompt is written, but how much of the real situation in your company it can see.
